utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Usher, please have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do the interpreters hear me? Good morning to Prosecution and to Defence counsel, to the accused, of course, and good morning to the witness who has just come in. We're going to call him Witness I. I ask you to remain standing for as long as it takes you to take an oath according to the formula which is being given to you by the usher. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may now be seated. You have come to The Hague -- we're going to call you Witness I because you are being covered by protective measures that you requested, and this explains why you are being positioned the way you are. First of all, you're going to hear the questions asked by the Prosecutor because you are a Prosecution witness. Then Defence counsel will ask you questions; he's on your left. Mr. Goran Jelisic is the accused. Then if the Judges wish to, they will ask you the questions they consider appropriate. Let me remind you that when you answer, turn to the Judges. The questions are asked from one side or the other, but when you give your answer, turn and face the Judges when you speak. The Prosecution has the floor. Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I have, usher, assistance in placing the summary of the witness statements in front of the him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness must identify his name without pronouncing it, to look at the piece of paper given to him. Look at the piece of paper and check to see that this is your name. If it is, please nod but do not say your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now please answer the Prosecutor's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Tochilovsky:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, is the summary before you the document which you had the opportunity to read and recognise as a correct summary of your statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, I would like to ask you first some questions on events before you were taken to Luka. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when the former mayor of Brcko, Mustafa Ramic, made an address to the citizens of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when the address was made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that address about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Should I tell you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in general, very shortly, what was that about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Mayor Ramic addressed the citizens of Brcko through the local TV station (redacted). He asked them to have tensions eased and to find, through peaceful democratic means, the best solution for the further coexistence of the citizens of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, were you detained on May 4, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who detained you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was detained by paramilitary formations or, rather, the Serb forces that had occupied our town in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other people who were detained with you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Most of them were Bosniaks, Muslims, and there were a few Croats as well. Also, there were people coming from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then and other people from your neighbourhood moved to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you then subsequently taken to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were taken with you to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: In half of the mosque there were between 80 and 90 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were those detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, I said that most were Muslims, Bosniaks. There were a few Croats and there were people coming from mixed marriages, for example, where the mother was a Serb and the father a Croat, or, for example, there was a man who was also named Goran who was with us in the mosque. I don't know what his ethnicity was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you treated during those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were angry with us. Some would get beaten up. They insulted us. They said that we should all be shot dead, that only five per cent of us should be allowed to live. Then somebody else would walk in and say that we should not worry at all, that they were only interested in the Green Berets, members of the SDA, those who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you provide the interrogators with any names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give the interrogators names of any people you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I did. I was forced to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you provided the interrogators with those names on which basis? What were the allegations about those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, they told me or, rather, they first gave me a piece of paper and a pencil. When they were interrogating me, they asked me to write down the names of those people in Brcko whom I knew to have weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you gave the names of people who were in possession of weapons or hunting weapons? What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At that moment, since I was threatened to be killed if I did not write down some names, I thought of writing down the names of those people for whom I was 100 per cent sure that they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those people afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Unfortunately -- I don't know it was because I wrote down their names -- out of the four men whose names I wrote down, two were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the names of those two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted). His name was Ahmed Fatic. The other one was called Hazim Vilic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Ahmed Fatic, (redacted) (redacted), was about 71 or 72. Perhaps he was even older than that. The other one, Hazim Vilic, was a bit younger than him. He was about 55 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you transferred to Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was transferred to the Luka camp from the barracks, where I was together with the others. We came from all local communes in the town, all of us who were in the barracks, and we were brought in on the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a man by the name of Goran Jelisic when you arrived to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the man? What did he look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was thin, taller than myself. He wore a police uniform, a summer police uniform of the former police. On one hand he had a bandage; I don't know if it was his right hand or left hand. When I first saw him, he brought in a plastic box and asked us to leave our personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When he entered the second time, of course, after having taken away this box with our personal belongings, and when he entered the second time, he walked in with a baton. It was a black rubber baton, perhaps one metre long. He hit it on the ground in order to call us to attention, and when we all looked in the direction where he stood, he said, "I'm the Serb Adolf," and he said his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any objection from any guard who was present there to what Goran requested of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? What kind of objections? Who did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: While Goran was asking us to put our personal belongings into this box, in the hangar, there was a man --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The translation doesn't follow. Maybe you can speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, the witness is speaking slowly enough.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There was a policeman there who stood in a camouflage uniform with a white belt, and at one point in time, he addressed Goran. He said, "Why were you taking their personal belongings?" He said this belonged to us and that it belonged to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Goran's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He said, "Have you handed them over to me?" That policeman said that he was responsible for our fate. Goran angrily left the hangar and went towards the administrative building. He came back and said to this policeman that there was a telephone call for him. This policeman never returned to guard us. They brought another soldier in an olive-grey uniform, and he put a machine gun in front of us. He had long hair; he was thin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, can you tell the Court what you know about the two brothers from Zvornik? What happened to them, very shortly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Among the personal belongings that we handed over to Goran Jelisic, there were our personal IDs as well; that is to say, our IDs, our driver's licenses, our passports, our money, and other valuables. When Goran came back afterwards, he was carrying something, I don't know if it was IDs, but at any rate, he had some documents. Then he said to us, "Now you are going to see how proven Green Berets are going to be treated." They came from Zvornik to fight at the Brcko front. He called out their names, he called out their names and surnames and said, "Get out, you Green Berets." They were twin brothers and they looked alike. They even wore the same clothes and footwear. Goran handed over one of them to Sok, Enver Sok, and Enver took one of the brothers into the premises of the administrative building. As for the other brother, Goran started beating him at the entrance to the hangar. The hangar door was ajar, and I was close to that door. One could see Goran beating one of the brothers with the baton. He was shouting at him, cursing him. The man was begging him, saying that he was not guilty of anything and that he should not beat him for nothing. All who were present in the hangar could hear that. The blows were strong and they resounded. There was silence. One could only hear Goran and the man whom he was beating up. That went on for about 10 or 15 minutes. After that, two shots rang out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, do you remember whether Sok asked Jelisic what to do with the other brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do remember. As Goran was coming back from the place from which he had picked up one of the brothers, he had in his hands a pistol, a Scorpio with a silencer, black. At that moment, Enver came out of the office and had with him the other brother, and he said to Goran, "And what am I to do with him?" Goran laughed and said, "Take him to the other one. They now need yet another one to play poker."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to that other brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Enver took him in the direction of the place where his brother was lying down. They went, Enver on his left-hand side and the other brother on his right-hand side, and they were walking towards each other. As they arrived two or three metres or so from the body of his brother, from where the body of his brother was lying, Sok stopped for a while and this brother went on. With his right hand, he lifted the pistol with the silencer and fired, and I don't know exactly where it was first, in the stomach and then at the back of his head or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, do you remember a man by the name of Jasce in Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court shortly what you know about his fate? What happened to him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I knew Jasce even before he was brought to Luka. However, in Luka, as I cued for the pass with the rest of the group of 30 or so of my townsmen, I saw them taking out Jasce. They took him out and led him into the administrative building. They tortured him there, ill-treated him, abused him verbally. Of course, I could hear it all because the doors of these offices were open, and they kept him there for some time. After that, when they took him out through the door, that is, in front of the door, one could see marks of harassment, that is, torture on him. His face was bloody, his hair was dishevelled, and he looked dazed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, when you refer to "them", "they" took him to the office building, who took him to the office building from the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I mean Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before Jasce was taken from the office building in that condition as you described, did Ranko Cesic ask anything of Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. He asked Goran and Enver, "Which one of you will take him over?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the response? Who responded to him and what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Goran said, "Give him to me," and, "He needs to load his gun again anyway."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then to Jasce?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They took him away also in the direction of those two executed brothers, and there with two shots at the back of his head and stomach. They also executed Jasce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a man by the name of Danijel in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, he was, but only for a short period of time. Danijel was brought -- I can't remember exactly who it was that brought him, but they took him in the direction leading from the main gate to the place where those three had been executed. Around me were people who had also been issued passes. We were standing in a very compact group so that it was more difficult for me to see what was going on. I need to point out that very near me, in my immediate vicinity, my brother, my elder brother, was also standing, and he kept saying to me all the time, "Don't look in that direction," and very angrily too. With his body he shielded me. He screened me from anything that I could see. I need to point out that. Otherwise, I and all the rest of us could not look directly but, rather, we had been ordered to keep our heads down. However, on the sly, as much as we could, we looked and we tried to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you mentioned that Danijel was taken and they took him to the place of execution, who took him to that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Who took him? Goran and Enver Sok took him away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened to this man when they approached the place of execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: You mean Danijel. We heard two shots, and he stayed lying down at the place where the others had also been killed. I only need to say one thing. After they would kill somebody, they would, every time, ask for volunteers to take away the body. Some who volunteered to take them away were not afraid and they volunteered. Some were designated by Goran himself. He would merely point with his hand, "You and you, take this one away." So when Jasce was executed, Goran indicated with his hand a man who was standing near the car. He was a Bosniak, a Muslim, and he was standing right next to the car. Goran called him out personally to take the body away. (redacted). Incidentally, he is an invalid. He has trouble with one leg. So he asked Goran, because he was an invalid and because he dare not look at that man, to pick out somebody else. However, two men volunteered and (redacted) (redacted). They picked up the body, Jasce's body, and took it behind the hangar down the street, and they left it there, I believe, on the right-hand side. I heard later that there was a heap there, a heap of dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness I. Were you rearrested after you were released from Luka camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you detained after you were rearrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: When I was issued a pass from Luka, my brother and I thought that it would be dangerous to go back to our neighbourhood community, and so we went to our friends (redacted), and we stayed at our friends' until the 14th of July. Then at 2.00 in the morning, I and other people from surrounding buildings were loaded onto the buses of the town transport and deported to the camp at Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Jelisic when you were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, but not when we arrived right away. There were some other people there. Goran was at Luka still, presumably. However, after perhaps a month or two, one day in the afternoon hours, Goran arrived at the camp at Batkovic. He was wearing a civilian uniform, nicely dressed. Outside the camp, that is, beyond the wire, there was a girl, a young woman, waiting for him. Around him -- about ten inmates gathered around him, and he talked to them. He was even inquiring if that dark one they used to call Ohro was there. Goran had come, planning to take two from the Batkovic camp, two inmates, I mean, to take them with him, two inmates who had also been at Luka. I think that the name of one was Muta, rather, the nickname of one was Muta. I, at that moment, was about a metre and half or two away from him. He also made some jokes on that occasion, naturally, as he knew some that he used to see at Luka before. So he waited for the two that he had come for to take some of their personal effects, and he took them away in all likelihood. Afterwards, after I left the camp, I heard that he needed then somebody who had been to the Luka camp to deny the news in the media about how Luka was a camp and that Goran was involved in executions. I also heard later that those men were forced, were coerced into making such statements to media, as were asked from them by Goran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just mentioned the name Ohro. Goran was looking for Ohro to take him with Goran for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I only need to say that he did not ask to take Ohro with him. He asked for the other two. But he asked about Ohro, by the way, because he used to be his assistant there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness I. Now I have some questions on the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: May I have the assistance of the usher?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. Tochilovsky, I'd like to have you state clearly what murders were acknowledged by the accused to which he pleaded guilty, that is, Count 14 and 15, I believe. Perhaps 16 and 17 as well. Are there any others in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness, as well as other witnesses, they are asked about those killings to which Goran Jelisic pleaded guilty to, but the main purpose of these questions we ask, and this witness was asked to explain that very shortly, because we are interested not whether the facts took place because Goran Jelisic pleaded guilty to that, but we're interested in how the killings were committed, what Goran Jelisic's behaviour was, what did he say, because all these facts are relevant to Count 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's what I wanted you to clarify. The Judges, as you know, want these proceedings to be very circumscribed to genocide. All right. Mr. Tochilovsky, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First, Exhibit number 12. You were shown this list before, and can you tell us what you know, very shortly, whether you know what happened to the person or not, and if you know, whether you saw an incident or not? Sakib Becirevic, on page 1. Do you know his fate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: His fate?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I heard about it after I left the Batkovic camp. I heard it from people who were detained in the gymnasium partizan at the time when Sakib was executed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second page, there is the name Ahmed Hodzic, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I need to correct you. It is Ahmet Hodzic. (redacted). Otherwise, they used to call him Papa. He, together with my family, were hid in the same cellar. We came out together. We were together in the Wooden Mosque at Kolobara. There they singled him out and took him to the health centre. At the health centre he was tortured and there they interrogated him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you heard from others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 3 there is the name Fadil Mujic. Very shortly, do you know what happened to this person, Fadil Mujic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). He was also at the mosque with me and was subsequently transferred to the barracks with me, and from the barracks to Luka. He stayed behind after I left Luka, and from people who were with him, I heard that one evening Fadil was called out and taken away and never been brought back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name is Galib Muranjkovic. Do you know what happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted). He thought that he would be saved if he went from Brcko to Janja. However, I also heard that he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name is Mirsad Pasalic. Witness I, I would like you not to mention if you find any relatives or close neighbours, not to mention the fact because it will identify you. Just tell the Court what you know, if anything, about the person I ask you. Do you know anything about Mirsad Pasalic, what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). I heard that he was taken off a bus when he was supposed to be transferred to Brezovo Polje and that he was killed as soon as he was taken off the bus. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 4, there is the name Mithat Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted). He was killed at his home, in his yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name is Kemal Sulejmanovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Kemal Sulejmanovic, that is the brother of Vasif Sulejmanovic. He was killed at the Laser company. That's what I heard from people who were brought from Laser to Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name is Osman Suljic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Osman Suljic, son of Enver Suljic, (redacted) (redacted). He was born in 1961. He was detained together with me at the mosque. They released him from Luka, and he went to the local community where he lived. He was there at home with his sick father. Also I heard from a lady from the neighbourhood that he was killed in his garden. She said that his throat had been slit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next names are the names of the Terzics, Ekrem Terzic, Enes Terzic, Muhamed Terzic. Very shortly, Witness, if you know what happened to those people, just tell us what you know, not about where they lived or who their relatives were, but just shortly, whether you know what happened to them. What happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were also detained at the mosque together with me. Afterwards they were transferred to the barracks, we were together over there too, and from the barracks, they were transferred to Luka. They were among the first to receive permits to get out from Luka. When they were leaving, when they were going home, they were waving their permits at us. For one period of time, they were staying with Enes's mother-in-law in the Serb part of town, and when they ran out of food, they went to Kolobara, the neighbourhood where they had lived. I heard that they were killed at home. I also heard about that from a lady in the neighbourhood who had been at home during those days. She told us that they were killed as follows: While an apartment was being looted, they were looking through the window and that the curtain on that window had moved. That revealed their presence, so they were taken out of the house and all three were killed. I heard about that from a woman, and if it is not absolutely necessary, I would not like to mention her name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move now to Exhibit 13. Again, very shortly, if you know what happened to these persons, just tell the Court. Number 1 is Midhat Sabanovic. What happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that he was killed in his own yard, by his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2 is also the person you already told the Court about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, but I didn't say everything about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard that he was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 5, there is the name Amir Novalic. Do you know or did you hear anything about what happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I knew him very well, and I heard from people at the Batkovic camp, and also at the Luka camp, that he was killed in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under number 9, there is the name Mustafa Medinic. Do you know what happened to this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: From the people in his street who were brought in that day to the Wooden Mosque, I heard that both brothers; that is to say, Mustafa Medinic and Ado Medinic, were killed at home because allegedly they had been accused of being snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you just mentioned number 10, Ado Medinic, as being killed. Now number 11, Irfan Topolcevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Irfan Topolcevic was also killed at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 12, Irfan Suljic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was also killed when Mustafa Medinic was killed and when Ado Medinic was killed, on that very same day, because they were neighbours. Also I learned of his fate in one of these three camps, the mosque, Luka, Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 15 is Muhamed Jakubovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Muhamed Jakubovic, nicknamed Ulika, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: (redacted). He made goods out of leather. He was killed at the gate of his own yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 16 is Sakib Becirevic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I knew that man too. I heard of his fate from people who were exchanged, and that is how they came to the federal part of the Brcko municipality. I heard about this from a man -- I know his name and surname -- and he said that Sakib was taken out of the Partizan gym. He took him out personally or, rather, Ranko Cesic took him out personally. He took off his handcuffs and said that he should jump over the fence. When Sakib did that, Ranko killed him. Allegedly, he said that this man had started to run away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The next number is 17, Sakib Edhemovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Everybody in Brcko knew that man. He was an excellent physician. He lived in the centre of town. I heard that he remained in the occupied Brcko and that he was killed around the middle of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next names are under numbers 19, 20, 21, and 22, the Terzic brothers and Kemal Sulejmanovic. Are they the same people you just talked about on the previous list as people being killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name is number 23, Vasif Sulejmanovic, 23. 24 A. (redacted) (redacted). In the beginning, when they were detained at the mosque, and I was present there as well, a Serb soldier took me out of the Wooden Mosque in the neighbourhood of Kolobara. He asked me about Vasif, whether Vasif had any money on him. This Serb's name was Milenko Radusic. I said to him then that I did not know. I assumed that his wife had taken the money away with her. Milenko Radusic said to me that he heard that same story from Vasif; however, he torched his house with a Zolja nevertheless. I saw Vasif a few times in Brcko before I was deported to the Batkovici camp. Afterwards I heard that he was killed during my stay in the camp of Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 27 is Muhamed Zelenjakovic. Is that the same person you just mentioned on the previous list?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I do not recall whether this was on the previous list, (redacted) too. He was also together with us in the Wooden Mosque in Kolobara and in the medical centre. He was also together with us in the barracks and in the Luka camp. He was released, but then he was killed at home together with his son, and his house was torched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 30, Ahmed (sic) Fatic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Just one correction: It is Ahmet, with a "T," Fatic. That is a man whom I put on that list of hunters who had rifles, and I said that he was over 70 years old. His next-door neighbour, a lady, came to see us after we left the Luka camp, and she told us that on one day, she had gone to see her neighbour because she got suspicious, as she was not seeing him around. However, as soon as she walked into the house, she smelt a stench. He lay in the room dead and the body had already started to decompose. She did not know whether he had been killed or whether he had died a natural death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next number is 36, Osman Vatic, the last name on this list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I knew Osman Vatic; I also knew his wife, as well as his two daughters. I did not know that he was at the Luka camp. During the war, I first saw him in the Batkovic camp. That is a man who had an artificial leg. I was personally present in the camp when, one day, an exchange was organised. Forty inmates from the Batkovic camp were supposed to be exchanged. A Serb officer then stopped the bus and said, "Take this Osman Vatic too so that we could get rid of him." They took him to Brcko, in front of the SUP building, together with the remaining 40 men. He was the 41st. They took him out in front of the SUP building and they killed him. That's what I heard from the men who remained in the bus at that point and later reached the free point of Brcko; that is to say, the federal part of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to take a 20-minute break and then resume with the cross-examination, I suppose, by Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, could I ask you initially, please, if during my questioning of you, if you do not understand the question which I ask you, please do not be shy. Tell me immediately that you don't understand the question and ask me either to repeat it or to rephrase it. Can you do that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, this concerning yourself: Prior to the commencement of the war, were you in any way involved in political life?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the war or since the war, have you become involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or joined a political party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, I did not. 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) 17 (redacted) 18 (redacted) 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted) 21 (redacted) 22 (redacted) 23 (redacted) 24 (redacted) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness I, can I now move to this, please: Between then and the time when you were detained, was there an outbreak of fighting in the Brcko district?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As of that day, the 1st of May, in the afternoon hours and until as time went by, we heard increasingly -- we heard evermore explosions and rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, when you were evacuated, did you see signs that heavy fighting had taken place in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By signs of heavy fighting, did that mean buildings that had been destroyed by artillery, large amounts of bullet holes on buildings and things like that? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I shall give you some information. During my stay, between the 1st and the 4th of May, that is, during my stay in the cellar, Serb forces brought in a tank to place near the health centre, and every couple of minutes or so one could hear detonations, rather, it would fire off and the door to our cellar would shake every time. The tank was about 70 or 80 metres away from the building in which I was. At that moment, that tank was targeting the suburban localities Klanac, Rijeka, Suljagica Sokak, and Dizdarusa. Every time it would fire and the cartridge would drop on the asphalt, one could hear the clinking sound of the shell. And from different directions, small bullets, that is, rifle bullets, would be aimed at roofs of the houses, facades, windows, so that a shell fell in my yard and caused damage to the roof, and felled a tree and cut the telephone wire, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question, Witness I. I don't want us to get too far away from genocide. I bring you back to that. Count 14, we are talking about Count 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I just explain, please? The reason I'm exploring the existence of fighting in the Brcko district in May is this: The Prosecution rely on a series of mass graves which were found. The Defence is entitled to explore, in our submission, whether there were casualties, people killed during the course of that fighting who might reasonably be expected, having been killed in the circumstances of war, to be placed in a mass grave, as is frequently the case during fighting, because the Prosecution are, no doubt, going to say that these mass graves represent simply the act of genocide. So the Defence is entitled to examine, we submit, whether or not there's an alternative source, as it were, for the people in the mass graves. That's the purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is an ambiguity, Mr. Greaves, not only in your questions but in those of the Prosecutor. I want to remind you that, as my colleagues appropriately pointed out to me, Goran Jelisic is not accused of complicity in genocide, he's accused of genocide. That is the Prosecutor's accusation, which is that Goran Jelisic, for the Prosecutor, had the intention of destroying a significant part of the Muslim population, which was Bosnian, for religious reasons. That's the Statute. Let us not redo the whole war in the area of Brcko. Jelisic allegedly committed genocide. The Judges are not the ones who put that accusation down; it is the Prosecutor. I'm not only bringing you back, Mr. Greaves, but also bringing the Prosecutor back to the count of genocide because the accused pleaded guilty to everything. That doesn't concern you directly, Witness I. Don't be concerned. These are legal discussions, but they're very important for the accused. I'm not criticising your work, Mr. Greaves. I simply would not like us to move too far away from Count 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I understand that. Can I just make this further explanation to Your Honour? The issue of numbers of people who were killed is one which is important. Your Honours have to decide inter alia whether, in fact, the numbers actually killed represents a sufficient or, as Your Honour described it, a significant part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Muslim population. So the issue of numbers is one which is important because if one is to demonstrate whether or not there was someone trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: -- to demonstrate by evidence that there is another source for the killings, in other words, fighting, in other words, that they were not, in fact, part of genocide, if there was a genocide, then that's a matter which goes and is relative and a probative issue which Your Honours have to try, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you know that the question of the conflict, I say this to the Prosecutor and to the Defence, the question of the conflict is one which has been discussed at great length. Let me remind you that even our Statute doesn't speak about a conflict but says that genocide means any of the following acts committed with the intent to destroy in whole or in part a national, ethical, rational, or religious group. I understand that one can discuss what the term "part" means or the word "part" means, but we have to know exactly what the accused is being accused of. For the time being, we are looking at Count 1, that is, genocide includes, and then the Prosecutor has to show that those acts were committed, not through direction of Republika Srpska but by Goran Jelisic with the intention of destroying, in whole or in part, a national, ethical, racial, or religious group. I do understand. This is the reason that I keep bringing you back. It's not because I have a mania about going quickly. If the trial has to be long and slow, then it will be long and slow, but it has to go back to the exact point, and this does not only concern you, Mr. Greaves, but it concerns the Prosecutor as well. Having said this, you explained what it is that you are attempting to do and we thank you for doing so. Please continue, but, like the Prosecutor, try to remain within Count 1. Goran Jelisic has not been accused of complicity of genocide. He has been accused of genocide itself, at least that is Count 1 as it stands today. Please continue. Thank you, Witness I, for your patience. Witness I, try to answer concisely when the questions are asked. Let me explain why I'm saying this. The Prosecutor and the Defence, in this judicial system which is our own, have a plan. They know where they are going. They have a purpose. Mr. Greaves is to defend the accused and the Prosecutor is to demonstrate what the accused is being accused of. The questions may seem a bit short to you, and you may feel that you have many things to say, but still try to answer the questions that are asked you in a very specific and concise matter. Please continue, Mr. Greaves. I myself have wasted some time, but I have done this with the agreement of my colleagues. We deemed that this was necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, may I just ask him about whether or not there were casualties there? That was the one question I wanted to ask. Your Honour didn't specifically rule on whether you considered that to be a relative and probative matter in the context of what I was asking, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, do ask your questions, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, again you can answer this very shortly: Were there obvious signs that there had been casualties, whether civilian or military, and by "casualties," I mean wounded or dead, in the signs of fighting that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There were no signs to show that people, that is, those who are in mass graves, were killed by shells. They were all killed in a bestial way only because they were Muslims or Croats, or because they had belonged to a party, or simply because they did not like that man, and if they happened to be at a certain place, they would be killed. Even if there were shelling casualties, their number is negligible. These victims didn't come from the town but from surrounding villages, because the heavy artillery, the Serb heavy artillery targeted Rahic, Palanka, Brka; that is, places outside the heart of the town, properly speaking. In the town, civilians perished in their own cellars, basements, homes, yards, camps, or were taken away to the Sava River and shot dead there, so that all the town casualties, 90 fatalities -- 99 per cent of the fatalities were killed at close range; that is, they were shot dead, their throats were slit, and by other methods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now, please, Mr. I, about your evacuation and removal to the medical centre. Is this right: that something like 150 to 200 people were moved in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, at about 12.00, Serb formations were going down the street on which I lived and they were using the loudspeaker, inviting us to come out of our houses and cellars. I suggested that it would be better for us to come out and go wherever they were inviting us to, that is, the health centre, rather than stay in the cellar. A stream of people, impotent, elderly women and children made the column, and I headed that column, and they brought us before the health centre. There, they separated women and children and with buses which were already waiting, they took them in an unknown direction, and men between the ages of 15 and 75 were kept in front of the health centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, you've given us an awful lot of information, but you've not answered the question which I asked you. Please, would you direct your mind to the question which I'm asking and answer that, please. Is it right that between 150 and 200 people were evacuated and taken initially to the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I would not call it an evacuation. From the cellar, we were brought before the medical centre so that we could be interrogated there, so that we could be beaten there, so that we could be killed there. They never showed any kindness to us. They beat us all, one after the other, both children and old men, sick and healthy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, you're going to be here a lot longer than is necessary if you don't answer the question. I don't mind whether we call it an evacuation or an exercise in moving people. How many people were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Well, that part of my neighbourhood community, it's about two streets. Men, we were about 150, maybe 200.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us in evidence just now that the age range was people between 15 and 75, as to those who were separated off and kept in front of the health centre. Isn't this right: that the group of people who were separated from you were women, children, and males under 18 and over 60, and, indeed, that is what you told the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Some. Some, those advanced age. They also dispatched women and children, but in the mosque --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've answered, Witness I. I think that was the question that Defence counsel was asking you. If he needs any further details, he'll ask you for them. Mr. Greaves, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst the people who were there, were there some, in fact, who were Serb men of working age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Office of the Prosecutor this: that you had been told by a Serb friend that the working male Serbs had been taken to the army barracks, that they had been mobilised. Do you remember doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know what I should call this. This man is from a mixed marriage. Yes, it is true that he's called Dragan. His father was probably a Serb and his mother a Muslim. He was together with us in the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you information to that effect, indeed, that those who would not go for mobilisation would be beaten and forced to eat grass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That I was told by someone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this right: that when you were at the mosque, you were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the people involved in that interrogation somebody called Mauzer and somebody called Kosta?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By "Kosta," is that somebody called Kosta Kostic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Later on I learned that that was his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a man of about 40; would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The subject of the interrogation which was conducted with you was, in effect, this: Mauzer wanting to know what you knew about people who were engaged in military activities, people who possessed weapons, people who belonged to the political parties; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as two, at least, of the people whose names you gave as possessing weapons, although you don't know why they were killed, the information is that they were subsequently killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all four were hunters, but only two were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described in evidence somebody called Danijel having been killed at Luka. Had you seen him before at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him at the mosque. He was taken to the medical centre where they interrogated him and where they beat him, together with Ahmet Hodzic, Papa, and the Terzic brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ahmet Hodzic, was he beaten because he was involved in politics in the area? Was that the focus of why he was being ill-treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was president of the local community, and he was a member of the SDA. The soldiers who were present there -- rather, one soldier said publicly, "Why don't you say that you're president of the party? Why don't you speak up?" And he said he was only a member of the party, and then they said, "Get out," and they took him away and he never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about Danijel? Was there any reason for the beating that was given to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Danijel was accused of having had a Scorpio gun at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a young man of military age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: He was a military-aged man; however, as far as I know, he was not involved in anything. I knew him personally from way back. I knew him as an exemplary citizen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it within your knowledge, Mr. I, that other people whilst at the mosque were interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again was the focus of those interrogations to obtain information about organisation of resistance, possession of weapons, money, property, things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: All the time they were looking for snipers who did not exist; they looked for weapons which did not exist. I know a few men whom they had beaten up, having accused them of having owned weapons, and I can guarantee that these persons did not have weapons. So that was just used as a pretext for mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right, Mr. I: Some information was given to them by somebody called Jasmin, some of Fikret, the green grocer, nicknamed Binto, and from a man called Midhat Kobilja, who gave them a list of people who owned weapons and who were SDA members?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, there were such men who agreed to talk in order to save their lives, to say what was true and what was not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay at the mosque, somebody called Suljic was killed trying to escape, and somebody, I think, also managed to escape completely, Enes Turkusic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Exactly. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly one question which I hadn't asked you about your own interrogation. Is this right: that (redacted) (redacted) you were singled out almost immediately to go and be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, as a result of your interrogation, you were asked about a particular shooting club, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not try to tell them that the only weapons that were held by this shooting club were, in fact, air guns, air weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. I thought that this shooting club only had air guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken to the shooting club and a search was conducted with you there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No, a search was not conducted. Everything that was in this shooting club was driven away in automobiles, in the direction of Bijeljina. There were some technical goods there, television sets, video recorders, telephones. There were air guns, small-calibre ammunition, and guns for competitions, M48s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: M48 rifles, which is not an air gun, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's right, but there weren't many of those. There were a few of them only. However, this shooting club sometimes competed with such rifles as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To put it very shortly, in one compartment, 8 cases of ammunition, 5.000 rounds of small-calibre ammunition, 15 small-calibre pistols, 2 large-calibre pistols, walkie-talkies, small-calibre rifles, and hunting rifles, those were also recovered, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I cannot recall hunting rifles, but you're right as for the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After Ahmet Hodzic, otherwise known as Papa, had been taken away, did the man Jasmin, who is the son of the green grocer, give them further information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At this moment I cannot recall precisely, because I was not present, but I believe that he might have said something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He named two particular individuals who had owned weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. He did give names and these persons were taken for interrogation to the medical centre, and then they were brought back too. It was quite visible that they had been mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right: that the Terzic brothers were at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: The Terzic brothers -- the Terzic brothers were at the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right: Before they interrogated one of the brothers, they had already found two sniper rifles at their cousin's house, Nermin Terzic, and they were beating the brothers because of their relationship to this man, where rifles had been found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's right, but I have to point out that this relative of theirs had these weapons registered, and he was fond of hunting and was fond of fishing too. As for his weapons, they knew about it at the SUP too, where there were records concerning the possession of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this also right: that you were questioned at one stage by a man called Milenko Radusic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that someone, a sniper, had been found on the roof of Vasif Sulejmanovic's house and that action had been taken against the sniper's position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It's not any rifle. He asked Vasif for money, this Milenko did, and that's why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Answer specifically. The question was whether a sniper rifle was found. You say "Yes" or "No," or are you saying "not at all," that you don't know, or that you -- what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's some misunderstanding. What I'm suggesting is whether it's right or wrong, someone had told him that a rifle had been found and that that was the cause for an attack on the house, not whether it's true or not. He hasn't quite answered the question which I asked. Perhaps I can just deal with it quickly again. Just listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Rephrase the question. Perhaps I didn't understand it quite right either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether it's right or wrong as to whether there was a sniper on the roof, that was the accusation being made concerning Vasif Sulejmanovic's house and that's what you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same person who told you that explained that as a result of that being suspected, it had been attacked with an anti-tank launcher?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's not what that person had told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The reason I ask you is that's what you told the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993, January 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I remember. I remember that Milenko Radusic took me out of the mosque and asked me about Vasif Sulejmanovic, whether he had any money, because this Milenko Radusic was not interested in anyone who had weapons, he was only interested in money, gold, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn next to this please, Mr. I. During your detention at the mosque, is this right, that a group of Serb doctors were brought to the premises and people were treated for injuries and any illnesses that they might have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Some doctors came. I don't know whether all of them were Serbs. At any rate, at one point in time they allowed them to enter and bandage those who had wounds on their heads or other parts of their bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, you were taken to the military barracks. Was that all the people in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken to the barracks so that others could be brought to the mosque. Some stayed behind after me in the mosque and also at the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the barracks, were there already people there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. They were mostly people from the heart of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like your group, were they men of military age, that is, between 18 and 60?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The majority?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. There were women too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And amongst those detained at the barracks, also some Serbs. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Are you referring to the detained Serbs or the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Detained Serbs, Mr. I.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, from mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help me with this? At the barracks, was the person who was known as Jasce, Jasmin Cumurovic, was he there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he singled out of the barracks because of an allegation that he'd spat at a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. He was not singled out. This person who then saw him recognised him and said, "You there, go for a walk. Don't make me drill you with bullets." He said, "Why?" This other man replied that long ago, in a cafe, he spat at a girl called Ljilja, his relative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that somebody called Dragan Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, Tanaskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him at Luka, Tanaskovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your transfer to Luka camp. How many in all of you were transferred to Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: There were about five buses belonging to the public transportation company, the Laser Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would this be right: that about 300 people were transferred to Luka with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I assumed there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry. Would Your Honour just give me a moment? I've lost my notes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Significantly more than 300?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I cannot exactly tell, but there were really quite a few of us. When we entered the hangar half of us were there, one next to another, pushed against one another, so I cannot exactly estimate how many there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you placed immediately into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. First when the buses arrived in Luka they were stopped. We waited for some time in the buses, perhaps for someone to come. However, after that they would open the front door next to the driver and then we would leave one by one, entering the hangar. Near the entrance was a box which was a paper box at first, and then Goran brought a plastic box. However, since this was slow, they let us all into the hangar and then afterwards they started taking away our personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were put into the hangar were there already people there who had previously arrived at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. At least not in that room. I don't know about the rest. I only know that we were ordered to take brooms, some of us, and to sweep the floor in that room. There was quite a bit of glass, because the bridge is nearby, and this glass was broken due to the detonation when the bridge was destroyed. So some people cleaned this up. Then we had to sit down, and we had to keep our heads down. We had to look at the floor, and we had to keep our hands behind our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to move to a slightly different topic. I wonder if that's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We agree. We will resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before the cross-examination continues, two points: First, it's been brought to our attention that with all the witnesses, not just this witness, when we go into the lists, there's a difficulty for the administration because of the amount of redaction or editing of the material that has to be undertaken by your staff, and despite all their conscientious industry, it's very difficult for them to catch all the relevant passages that may offend the privacy that's being kept for the witness's evidence. It has been raised as a possibility that we might deal with questions about the list in private session. We're, obviously, all loathe not to have as much of the trial as possible in private, but seeing the scale of the difficulties that they're facing, I'm certainly content to make that application, if it otherwise finds favour. The second thing that I'd like to mention very diffidently, and I do it so as to save Mr. Tochilovsky the responsibility of irritating you, if I do irritate you, but it's this: I'm very concerned about the length of cross-examination. It does seem to me that a lot of the questions that are being asked are not cross-examination at all but are repeat questions which simply have the purpose of taking time. Now, in a case like this or in evidence like this where, for example, a witness is given a name that the defendant associated with himself, one of the things we need to know is that accepted, that he described himself in that way, or is that challenged, but those things aren't being dealt with, and all we're having is repetition. Sorry to sound a critical note, but seeing the passage of time, I thought it my duty to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps there's an interpretation problem. I didn't quite catch the end of what was said from the French interpretation. When a witness has given a name -- could you rephrase that, please? I didn't quite understand that. I'll ask my interpreter to pay particular attention to the interpretation of what the end of your sentence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, and perhaps I can rephrase it. One of the useful functions of cross-examination is this: Where evidence is given, for example, that a person uses a particular name to describe himself or where evidence is given that the defendant has said something about his intention, one of the useful purposes of cross-examination is to discover if that's accepted or if it's being suggested that that is incorrect, because then we all know where we stand. There may not have been very substantial identification of issues with this particular witness in that way. What we've had instead is repetition of the evidence or that sort of thing. That's what's troubling me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the first point, I will confer with my colleagues very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, first of all, would you like to respond to what your colleague on the Prosecution side said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no objection to us going into private session when the issue of the list of people is discussed. I think this morning particularly demonstrated the practical difficulties, and I criticise nobody in respect of that. They can arise because of relationships or people living next to one another or whatever it is. So I have no problem about that, and Your Honours may think that's an entirely practical suggestion, although I would echo my learned friend's suggestion that as little as possible should be done in secret; as much as possible should be done, as a matter of principle, in open court. But I understand the practical difficulties that are raised by that. As to the second matter, I reject entirely the accusation of professional misconduct which has been made against me, and I resent it and do not accept it. Your Honour, the cross-examination this morning has been made lengthy, not because I have been asking repetitious questions but because the witness would not answer the question which he was asked. I, therefore, reject the suggestion that was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have decided that henceforth, the review or examination of the two lists will be done in private session. I am saying this for the public gallery. There are quite a few people here in the public gallery who are listening to us today. Only some aspects could cause that to be the case, for example, that the questions deal with the list that could be prejudicial to the witness. We are also concerned about the length of the cross-examination, and the Judges are mindful of the need to conduct the proceedings according to Rule 90(G); that is, "(i) to make the interrogation and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth; and (ii) avoid needless consumption of time." The Judges wish -- I repeat, they wish -- that the time of the cross-examination, as much as possible -- I want this to be properly indicated -- as much as possible be matched with the length of the examination-in-chief, of course, with a degree of flexibility and suppleness which is to the advantage of the accused. Otherwise, it would be very easy for the Prosecution to conduct the examination-in-chief for three minutes and then to say to the Defence that he has only three minutes to cross-examine the witness. The Judges have been given certain powers by the texts and will apply those powers. I won't even say the rule; I'll say the principle applied with as much care as possible, that as much as possible, that should be our criterion and this is the way we should go, that the time of the cross-examination, as much as possible, should be -- I repeat, as much as possible -- matched with the length of the examination-in-chief. Then we move to Rule 90(H), that the "cross-examination shall be limited to the subject-matter of the direct examination ..." This is a fundamental rule. Naturally, the Prosecutor has called in his witness, brings out a certain number of points, and the cross-examination is to deal with those very points. Obviously, I am not unaware of the fact, and this is the third question, of the need to discuss the credibility of the witness, but the examination-in-chief is not limited to any points; therefore, the cross-examination must be able to bring out any questions of credibility as well. Lastly, I would ask Mr. Greaves not to have the witness repeat things needlessly. Questions can be asked simply by saying, "You said this during your examination-in-chief," and then we're going to go into subsequent questions which you might consider to be appropriate. This is how we feel that we could try to be sure that by the 17th, Friday, the presentation of the Prosecution's case could be completed. Last point, and in agreement with my colleagues, these Rules which now apply to the Defence will apply mutatis mutandis to the Prosecution when the Defence calls in its own principal witnesses. We can now continue, and I say to the public, this is the cross-examination of a protected witness whom we are calling Witness I. Mr. Greaves, you may proceed. Let me ask you right now to tell us approximately how much time you will need. You've used up about an hour and fifteen minutes, an hour and ten minutes. I think that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You took one hour. So you have been cross-examining for an hour, but you must acknowledge that the Prosecution, with its own witness, used how much time?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They used one hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, of course, we are not going to impose a necessity to finish within the next ten minutes. We are applying these Rules with flexibility and in the full respect of the rights of the accused, and that is why we're asking approximately how much more time you need? I will also ask the witness to answer more concisely, as far as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think to be fair, it was closer to an hour and a half that the Prosecution took for this witness this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must say, Mr. Greaves, that I thought it had lasted -- I thought that it lasted about an hour and a half. Are you sure, Mr. Registrar, when you give us these numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I thought we started promptly this morning and it finished at about 11.25, which is as near as you care to wish to an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I return to the difficulty of witnesses not answering questions? I'm going to make it plain that I'm not going to interrupt witnesses whilst they are speaking, because I know that the next objection that will come is that I'm harassing the witness. It really has to be for Your Honour to draw to the witness's attention as soon as he starts to stray from the question. If you look at the questions I'm asking, they're about two lines on average, in length. They're directed to a specific topic. The problem continues to be that the witnesses do not answer the question which they have been asked but answer some question which they would like to have been asked. So I'm not going to start interrupting them halfway through, because I know the allegation is then going to be, "You're harassing them," and that's unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We're not talking about harassing the witness. You can interrupt the witness. That's your right. We've seen this in other trials in this Tribunal. But it is true that we all, I'm not specifically speaking to Witness I but, Witness, I must know that this Tribunal has got some history behind it now and whether it's the Judges, the Prosecutor, or the Defence or Prosecution, we are very sensitive to the suffering that you experienced. We're familiar and understand what happened to you in this dreadful hangar where you were, and it is rather cruel and savage to say to a witness abruptly, "You're not answering the question." That's why we try to apply our rules with flexibility, but I am asking you to try to focus. The Defence must be able to do its work and it's work is to defend the accused. That's what a judicial institution in a democratic society does. I really ask you to focus on the questions and to answer the questions. When you want to develop something, I cannot interrupt you too much when you're speaking about what you experienced, but in the future I won't hesitate to do so to some extent because those are going to come after you, the other witnesses, the other victims, must also have time to express themselves. Do you understand what I'm saying? Do understand me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll -- Mr. Greaves, you did not give an answer about how much time you think you need to complete your cross-examination if the witness answers properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I anticipate being done in under an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope it really will be under an hour. I ask that it be that way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, you told us this morning about some glass that you found in the hangar, which was broken. Just very quickly, there was around the top of the hangar a line of windows. Did it come from those windows? Were the windows broken when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves, he wanted to explain something. He said that the hangar has windows, there were explosions, and did these -- was that the cause of the broken windows. You don't have to -- that was already explained. I even noted that. So please move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as the numbers were concerned who were detained with you, was that 300 -- or have I asked that? I'm sorry. I've made a note there -- at Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I believe you asked that question already. I cannot give you the exact number, but I think -- my guess is there were more than 300.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of the day that you were there, were people released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they released after interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Some were interrogated at Luka and then were released. Some were interrogated at the mosque and then they were released. I mean, such as, for instance, brothers Terzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would those people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're speaking about the hangar, Witness I.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Some were released from Luka after interrogation, and some were not interrogated there and yet were released nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
