utterances.text: The people who were released from Luka, what proportion of the people who were detained with you were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Two groups were released. A smaller group of about ten people, and the second group, and I was one of them, between -- something between 30 and 40 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if they were issued with a pass or any document to enable them to be released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. They were issued passes which were printed and one only had to fill in one's name. I was issued that pass but it simply went -- came to pieces at the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "printed," is that typewritten or printed, as it were, by a printing machine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think it was a copying machine of a kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pass which you were issued with, was that signed in your presence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: These release documents were signed in advance, so all one did was fill in the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to read who it was who had signed your pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I only know there was a seal of Semberija Majevica, and as for the signature, it was illegible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had been released, did you use that pass in order to move about and make your way around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: With that pass I managed to come out with the rest of the group as far as the Es locality, but the next day they took them away and said they were not valid, and we were told that we had to go and be issued a different pass from the SUP. Ranko Cesic came and tore up those passes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now something about which you heard in connection with the murder of the brothers from Zvornik. Is it correct that you heard Goran Jelisic say that they had positively been identified as Green Berets, that they were Albanians from Kosovo who had come to fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't think that that question asked of me is correct. All he said was that they were identified as Green Berets and that we would see how they should be treated. He never mentioned Kosovo. All he said was that they were Albanians, that they were Sqiptars, and they came from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue. The answer's been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, with respect, I want to put something to him that is inconsistent with that, if you wouldn't mind, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you made a statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities on the 3rd of January, 1993, Mr. I. Do you recall doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Some of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement at the end of making it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that you concluded the statement with the following paragraph: "Finally I declare here that I have stated my personal observations, that all I have said is true and correct, and I shall confirm it with my signature, standing prepared to repeat what I have said in court or before a humanitarian organisation should there be need." Do you accept that's how you concluded that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: At the time I gave the statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovinan authorities, I had not taken any oath then. I needed time, in conversation with others who were present, to simply put everything in its place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Amongst those who were issued passes that day, did that include the brothers Terzic, the three brothers, Muhamed, Ekrem, and Enes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, the transcript has indicated there was no audible response, but I heard him say something. Could you please answer again, Mr. I? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: You want me to repeat my last answer? Yes, they were brothers Terzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they issued passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were issued passes with that group. They left before me. They waved at us with their passes as they left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the question of your brother being issued with an ID card or a pass came up and Goran Jelisic was there, is this correct: that the man, Dragan Tanaskovic, was also there and was watching what was going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that Goran Jelisic deferred to him when the issue of whether either just your brother or both of you were to be released, and Dragan Tanaskovic said, "Both of them"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think that, at the time -- Goran Jelisic had more sway at the time, but Dragan, since he knew him before that, asked him to release the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I would like the Defence, when they refer to the witness statement, just to refer to it correctly, because in the statement it says: "Goran glanced at him and Dragan said ...", and the witness was asked whether it is true that Goran asked permission and he was given permission. Instead it says, "Goran glanced at him," and that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, it would be helpful if my learned friend would intervene and correctly refer to the question I asked, which was: "Is it correct that Goran Jelisic deferred to him," not the word "asked."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: In the question it says "Goran Jelisic deferred to him when the issue of either just your brother or both of you were to be released." It's not in the statement. It's not there. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It rather depends on what construction you put on the act of glancing at someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have been alerted to this misunderstanding, and they will have these declarations tendered as exhibits at the proper time. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry. You'll just have to give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able, please, Mr. I, during the course of your detention at Luka on that day, able to overhear an interrogation carried out by Ranko Cesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I was pretty far away from the room or, rather, from the office where Ranko took the people he interrogated, so I only heard him cussing, and I heard moans from that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, later that day, hear Ranko Cesic saying something else concerning passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct: that he appeared from an office and demanded to know who it was who had been issuing passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he express anger on that occasion because passes had been issued to you and other people, and that they were members of the SDA? Whether he was right or wrong about the membership, he was angry about members of the SDA being released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I just have to say that I wasn't the member of any party. However, I imagine that he was angry because I had received a pass, because I was involved in an incident before the war, several years before the war, in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you told the Office of the Prosecutor is this, and I shall read it out so there is to doubt about what is being said: "While waiting to get a pass, Ranko came out and said, 'Who is issuing the passes?' Ranko was mad at me, I believe, because some of my friends and relatives were members of the SDA party." Do you recall telling the Office of the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I recall that. However, I assumed that he was angrier on account of me, because he didn't know my relatives at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what gave you cause to believe, as you told the Office of the Prosecutor, that he was referring not just to you but members of your family? Was it something which he said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Out of all my relatives that I know, only one was a member of the SDA party, but I doubt that Ranko knew that particular relative of mine. All the rest were not involved in parties at all or were members of the SDP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In due course, did you form a line in order to receive passes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: We did not form in a line. We stood in disarray, perhaps in two or three lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the course of waiting for your pass, did you become aware of two other people, inspectors, Petar Kaurinovic and Dragisa Tesic, in an office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct: that they were engaged in the task of checking some printouts from the SUP files?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I presume, because they were in a room that was just by the entrance, on the right-hand side, where there is a window and where there were curtains. Quite a few people got out of Luka with their assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is this: You were able to form the opinion, from what you could see, that it was they who were deciding who should be set free and they who were deciding who should be shot; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I cannot claim that which I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. I, what you told the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1993, was this: "While this was all going on, police inspectors Petar Kaurinovic and Dragisa Tesic were in the next office checking the printouts from the SUP files, and deciding with one nod of the head who was going to be set free and who was to be shot." That's what you observed, isn't it, and that's why you told the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: If necessary, I'm going to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like you to explain that answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: These two inspectors, they brought files from the SUP, from IDs that were in the SUP. Lists had already been made of persons who were undesirable in town. Goran went to this office and probably got IDs from them, that is to say, the IDs of persons whose documents were taken out, that is to say, these files. However, I cannot say that they were the ones who said who was to be shot and who was not to be shot, because I realised for myself that Goran, Sok, and Ranko had shot people dead without any IDs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about the time at Luka when Jasmin Cumurovic was taken by Ranko into a building. Do you recall seeing Goran Jelisic appearing and coming to talk to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it right that he said this: "Those who aren't guilty should not be afraid. I'm only interested in the Territorial Defence and Green Berets"? He also added that civilians would stay for awhile and then be released.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand the word "civilians" to mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I think that civilians are all of those who were in their homes, who were with their families, with their children, who were not at any front line or anything, simply those who were left to the mercy of the men who came from the outside, and people who were from the vicinity of the town of Brcko as well as from the town of Brcko itself. Naturally, these people were of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you help us, please, about this: You mentioned in one of the two statements that you made before giving evidence about Danijel, I think, Ibrahimovic being beaten at the mosque, but you did not mention anything about being a witness to his murder. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I knew that man in part. Although he lived in my neighbourhood, I saw him only a few times in my lifetime. During the aggression, I first saw him at the mosque. He was taken out of there and taken to the medical centre. They interrogated him there because he was accused of possessing a Scorpion gun. After that, while I was at the barracks, I did not see him because most probably he stayed back at the medical centre. However, in Luka, I did see him in the afternoon. It was already getting dark. He was brought in from the main entrance to the Luka camp, and he passed by our group where we were waiting for passes, and then he was taken away to be liquidated. I have to draw your attention to the following: I did not exactly see who killed him, whether it was Goran or Enver, because my brother, who was very close to me, he shielded me with his body and said that I shouldn't look in that direction. I presume that he thought that some of the guards could have seen me watching this and then I could have been liquidated because of that. When I heard two shots, I managed, between my brother and another man, to glance in that direction. Danijel lay 20 or 30 metres away from us. He was wearing a leather jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, you haven't answered the question, with respect. Why was it that the only mention you make in your statements of Danijel was about him being beaten at the mosque, and you made no mention whatever about his murder? Don't go into the details of it again. Just answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is under point 18 of the summary, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. The summary isn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the statement to Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In the statement to Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. I haven't mentioned the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. To the authorities, yes. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I shall answer that question. I was not sure who had done it. That's why I didn't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already explained the contradictions between one statement and the other. Let me remind you of that, Mr. Greaves. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one other matter to put to him that -- I'm sorry. I hadn't realised Your Honour was speaking to one of your other Judges. Your Honour, there is one other matter which I want to ask him about as to why that doesn't appear, if he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You claim to have seen Goran Jelisic at Batkovic camp, and you told us the circumstances of that. In the statements which you made, firstly, to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities and to the Office of the Prosecutor, why didn't you mention that visit, Mr. I?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Because I think that it is necessary for me to say, at least now, that that man was killed on that day; however, unfortunately, I did not see who had killed him. I just saw Goran and Enver coming back from the murder scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That isn't the question that you were asked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't understand. Please, could you clarify this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's quite simple, Mr. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves will rephrase his question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have given evidence of having seen Goran Jelisic at Batkovic camp and the circumstances surrounding that visit. You did not refer to having seen Goran Jelisic at Batkovic camp in either your statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities or to the Office of the Prosecutor. Please can you explain to Their Honours why, if that was a matter which was sufficiently important for you to tell us about it, you didn't mention it on those previous occasions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I can give you a quick answer to that question. The reason is the following: The Bosnia-Herzegovinian authorities, when they questioned me, they were only interested in Luka, not in the Batkovic camp. Also when I gave this other statement, they were only interested in Luka. When I wanted to say what else had happened in the camp, they said, "That's not necessary."

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honours can give me a moment, something has just been drawn to my attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, a problem has arisen which I think I'd like to have discussed in the absence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without the witness or in a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Without the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask Mr. Greaves and Mr. Nice or Mr. Tochilovsky to approach the Judges with an interpreter and to explain what is at stake. Otherwise, we're going to use up a lot of time having the witness go in and out of the courtroom. I would like to have an interpreter and speak with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness I, please take your headset off and please remain seated. Mr. Greaves, this is a decision which is very pretentious. We have lost a lot of time in this case, and the Judges are mindful of the fact that the accused has rights, but they would like your position to be perfectly justified, and if it isn't, the Judges obviously would draw the proper conclusions in the future. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I draw your attention to the last answer which the witness gave, which is this: The reason he gave for not having discussed the matter beforehand was that in the two statements he gave, those questioning him were only interested in Luka camp. The statement which he has made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities contains in the original version, but not in the English version which was disclosed to us, a section which clearly reveals that this witness was being asked about both Luka and Batkovic. The English version reads in the following way: It gives at the head, at the top of the page, an indication of who it is who's taken the statement. It then gives a date and the legal basis for taking the statement, and then there's a line which says "Record of witness statement," and then there's a section which is written in English, which is not contained in the Bosnia-Herzegovina statement, which describes the legal authority for giving of such a decree. What, in fact, is missing is a paragraph containing ten lines which details what it was the person was being asked about and who he was, and it's that passage that contains in the original but not in the disclosed English version the fact that this witness was being asked about Luka and Batkovic. It's not in the English version. I've had a quick look at similar statements that have been disclosed to us, and as far as I can see, and my recollection is that no statement contains that similar section. I'm told that the Bosnian versions all contain that. The consequences of that are that those who have to work from the English version are being deprived of what is plainly an important part of what should have been disclosed, and what it appears is that editing has taken place, editing which cannot be justified on the grounds, for example, of national security, which has prevented the English-speaking member of the Defence from knowing properly what, in fact, the full contents of this statement is. As I say, it seems to me that this applies to all the other statements of a similar nature which have been disclosed to us. Your Honour will see from the last question and the last answer that was given that if that had not been brought to my attention, I would have been deprived of knowing what it was he was asked about. Of course, that represents a considerable unfairness to the defendant because quite clearly the paragraph in the Bosnian language version reveals that, in fact, that's what they were directing his attention to. Your Honour, my concern is this: We need to know how many other statements contain passages which have been excised, and that excision needs to be rectified immediately because, otherwise, we cannot continue properly to prepare our case if improper and inadequate disclosure has taken place, and if for some reason someone has excised from each statement potentially valuable information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tochilovsky?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to make some corrections to what was said by the Defence. The statement was given by the witness to the Bosnian authorities in Bosnian, not in English. The original document is in Bosnian. According to 66 of our procedures, the statements disclosed to the Defence should be disclosed in the language the accused understands. The statements were disclosed in Bosnian, which both the accused and its lead counsel understand, their native language. The English version of this statement is actually our internal document which was prepared for our investigators, because our investigators don't understand Bosnian. They don't speak Bosnian. So those statements which were taken by he Bosnian government in Bosnia were translated into English. So according to our obligation, we disclosed to the Defence the original document in Bosnian with all paragraphs. It is in the possession of the Defence. The Defence has had the opportunity to read it and to interpret it in any way they want. With regard to that English version which was prepared for our internal consumption, let's say, if Defence is not satisfied with the quality of that translation, they can return to us all this English translation because it's not disclosure of statement. Disclosure of statement is disclosure of statement in Bosnian. With regard to this specific paragraph, I think that that paragraph was taken away, because it is -- if you look at that paragraph, it is information which identified the witness. It starts with his name, with the place of birth, date of birth, the number of his identity card, where he lived, what was his -- where he worked, who were his relatives. At the end of this paragraph, which is separate, it is not part of the body of the statement, it is the introduction paragraph about the identity of the person, and this paragraph says that the witness was asked -- such and such witness with this identity, he was asked about events which happened in the town of Brcko, camp Luka and Batkovic, in Gornji Rahic and so on. So this paragraph, this information, contains identity information. It was taken out, I think, by our investigators, but the statement, the original statement, was disclosed without any redaction. As we received it from the Office of the Prosecutor, it was entirely in the same format disclosed to the Defence, and Defence has it in Bosnian, in the original language of the statement, in the language that both the accused and lead counsel understand. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect, my learned friend has just answered the point that he made. It has nothing do with concealing the identity of the witness if in the original all that information is given to the Defence in any event. So the point that he's making about this is the reason why it's done is absolute nonsense, with respect to him. Secondly, can I draw Your Honours' attention to the rule which governs disclosure of potentially exculpatory material, which is Rule 68, and the terminology of that Rule. It reads as follows: "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the Defence the existence of evidence known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence." Your Honour, it is under that rule which potentially inconsistent statements are disclosed, because that is evidence which may affect the credibility of a witness. Your Honour, that is the entire text of the rule, as I understand it. It makes no mention of disclosure under that Rule being made in a language which the defendant understands. The Rule which does mention that is Rule 66, which confines itself to two classes of documents. Rule 66 says: "Subject to the provisions of Rules 53 and 69, the Prosecutor shall make available to the Defence, in a language which the accused understands ..." And it then identifies two categories of documents. This document does not fall into either of those two categories, with great respect. And, Your Honour, those who framed the rules must clearly have had in mind that that requirement concerning language should be specifically restricted to those classes of documents. Your Honour, we submit again that there has been a disclosure of a document which has been edited in a way which is not justified by the needs of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Greaves. The statement that was made before the Bosnian authorities, was that statement given to you in a language that the accused understands and Mr. Londrovic understands in its most complete form, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to Mr. Londrovic, who is the lead counsel. Did you have that statement? Mr. Londrovic, answer us. Did you have the statement made to the Bosnian authorities, and you read each of those in order to bring out contradictions between that statement and the statement made to the Prosecutor? The entire statement, did you have it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: I personally did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did Mr. Greaves have the complete statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, in the English version of a statement that he had, he did not have the complete text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you chief counsel, are you lead counsel, Mr. Londrovic, for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am lead counsel, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have an interpreter paid by the Tribunal to facilitate your work with your co-counsel, Mr. Greaves, in the team, "Yes" or "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now turn to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add one matter, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But one point, one point, because we've lost a lot of time now. We've spent a lot of time. I'm going to give you the right to speak -- to say one point and only one. Then we'll take a break. Mr. Londrovic is the leader. He's had the version in Serbo-Croat since the beginning. It's up to you to coordinate things. In all the trials here, it is frequently the Serbo-Croat part that does the cross-examination when it is a Serbo-Croatian-speaking witness. It's not our fault that you are speaking English and only speaking English. I ask you to deal with the one point and only the one point that you can speak about now. We're wasting a lot of time, and I'm not prepared to continue wasting this much time. One point and one alone. Quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, the registry does not pay for documents which are already placed in the hands of the Defence, in English, to be translated again and it's impossible for us to secure that. We do have an interpreter, but we have not been given permission to have documents which have been given to us in English retranslated, because she would simply not be paid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I think that you have an interpreter. First of all, you had a statement in Serbo-Croat. It was given to the Defence team's leader, Mr. Londrovic. You have a translation system and interpretation system. There are contradictions or perhaps there are gaps in the translation. This is not the problem for the timing of the Judges. We've wasted a lot of time. We're going to take a 15-minute break, and we will resume with the cross-examination, and I will ask you to complete it within a minimal amount of time, 15 minutes at the most. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pursuant to 90(G) and 90(H), to which I would like to refer you but which I've quoted several times already, Mr. Greaves, I ask you to finish your cross-examination in 15 minutes. We grant you 15 minutes to complete your cross-examination. Thank you. It is about a quarter after, twenty after four. We give you 15 minutes to get to the essentials about what was dealt with in the examination-in-chief. Please proceed. The floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. I, I'd like to turn now, please, to the list of people about whom you were asked in examination-in-chief, and if I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ordinarily, we would move into a private session when we deal with the list, at least that's what we decided a few moments ago, and I think everybody agreed. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, I ask that this be in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it true that the Muslims constituted the majority of the population of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those areas that were shelled, were they Serb-populated areas or not? Were the areas shelled Serbian-populated areas or Muslim-populated areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb areas were not shelled at all. The shells were aimed at areas and at places such as Brka Palanka, Rahic, Maoca, and other suburban settlements such as Dizdarusa, Klanac, Begovaca, Brod, which were almost exclusively Muslim, Suljagica Sokak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question is: In an answer to the Defence, you said some Serbs from mixed marriages were among those detained in the barracks. Does it mean that those Serbs were married to non-Serbs, including Muslims? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "mixed marriages"? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I suppose a Serb mother and father, a Muslim, or the other way around. Those people were released immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are almost finished with your testimony, Witness I, but I know my colleagues have a few questions to ask. Let me first turn to Judge Riad. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness I. I would just like to understand some certain things, and perhaps you can help me. You were detained on May 4, 1992. Do you have an idea why you were arrested or detained? Did they tell you or did you try to find out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I still don't know why. I had a number of friends among people of other origin. That is, I had more Serb and Croat friends than Muslims before the war. My father brought up me that way, not to distinguish people between their ethnic origin, only to distinguish between good and bad people. Unfortunately, when it started in Brcko, I was surprised to see how those friends of mine behaved. That is, not all of them but some of them would pass me by without even saying hello. I didn't expect anything more than that, just, "Hello," from them, but somebody -- somebody instilled, somebody imparted a hatred, somebody instilled hatred in their subconscious and they practically changed overnight. A few months before that -- a couple of months before that we would go to discotheques, coffee shops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned also that a few years before you had an incident in a cafe. Was that with Serbs? Did you take a stand against the Serbs in this incident in the cafe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No. That incident was of a short duration. Quite simply, the place was about to close and I was about to go home, but Ranko Cesic came up, and he was quite under the influence, and we had an argument and he slapped me in the face. So I, of course, paid him back. That was why I was afraid that he might see me in Luka. But that happened two years before the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: That had no relation with your arrest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was only for ethnic reasons, because you are a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So why did they hate after that, because, as you said, you denounced four people? That was the reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I doubt that that was the reason. No. They would have released me immediately, because a couple of days had passed since I gave those four names. So that was not the reason. The reason was that I was a good friend, a good chum of that Dragan Tanaskovic, and when he got home he told his mother that he had seen me at the barracks, and she told him that he should go and find me and not to come home without me. It was his mother, because she was very fond of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Can I understand that if it was not for this friend, for this Serb friend, you would not have gone out, or anybody else would not be liberated if he did not have a Serb friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the man named Danijel Ibrahimovic was detained because he had a Scorpion military gun and then he was liquidated. Was this one of the reasons why people are liquidated or it could have happened even without that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: It could have happened even without that, and in many instances that was the case, even without it. Quite simply -- I shall give you an example. In the building in the Es settlement, and then next to that building there was another building, and they took away a guy from that building -- and he was the state champion in kayak -- only because he was good looking, because he was an athlete, and because he had a good car.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So that was also a reason for being liquidated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It could happen to anyone, is that what you want to say? To the rich and to the poor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I can give you another example. At Luka, at night, when it was dark you can't really see who's who. They simply pull somebody by his sleeve and say, "You stand up." They don't know who he is, they can't see him, but they take him away and liquidate him. Or just kicks him, pushes him with his foot and says, "You stand up." There were quite a number of such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When they stand up, what do they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Nothing. They simply take him out and shoot him dead. He had no right of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Because he was a Bosniak or a Croat. I did not spend a night at Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Question inaudible]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: For no other reason. Only because he was a Bosniak or a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness I, good afternoon. I have basically two questions I want to ask you. You said that when you were in the mosque, he said that only five per cent should remain. Did I understand you correctly? These are my questions: Who said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: They were getting into the mosque non-stop. Soldiers in uniform were getting into the mosque non-stop. They had different insignia. Some belonged to Seselj, others belonged to Arkan. There were quite a few of these paramilitary formations. As they would enter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But were these paramilitary, or military Serbian formations, or were they others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About whom did they say that? Five per cent of whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Five per cent of the total population of Brcko, of Bosniaks. Only Bosniaks and Croats were referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did they only want to leave five per cent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: That would be enough people for them to sweep the streets and to work in night-shifts. So it is this hard labour that these people would do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That basically was my first question. My second question is the following: You also said, about the two police inspectors who were involved in the Bosnian authority's interrogations, I believe that you spoke about a list of people who were supposed to be released or killed because they were not desirable in life. I'm not sure that I understood that correctly. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is whether you know who drew up the list.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'll give you a piece of information. When I was released from Luka and when I was in Es, a Serb friend came to pick me up. He wanted me to turn his TV set on by using a battery. His name was Zoran Markovic. At that time in Brcko, there was no electricity in private buildings and apartments, and a football game, a soccer game, was being played for the cup. He came to pick me up to make it possible for him to watch the game. As I was sitting in his room, he showed me a list of persons, the names of persons whom he was supposed to liquidate, but he said to me that he phoned these people at night, not exactly all of them, telling them to hide, to go away. Everything was planned in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By whom? Everything had been planned in advance. Who planned all of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I don't know who the main person in charge of this project was, but when you put all these things together in a certain order, I think that the national parties are to be blamed for it, that it's the fault of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The people in the mosque who said only five per cent should be left, the two police inspectors who had a list of people who had to either be killed or released, did those people have any relationship with Goran Jelisic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: As for these people in the mosque, I'm not sure. As far as those in Luka are concerned, I imagine it could be so, because Goran Jelisic didn't know these people in Brcko. Somebody had to point them out to him and to say who was who, to set these ID cards aside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something else with which I will finish. You spoke about the list -- well, everything that you say to me now did you already say before either to the Prosecutor or to the Bosnian authorities, or is this the first time that you're speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'm speaking about this at length.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are you speaking about this for the first time today in more detail? Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I'm only going to tell you one thing. When I made my first statement to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, I gave it for three days. The man who was questioning me said that my statement was more important than that of any other inmate. However, he did not have the patience to work with me any longer. He was too tired, exhausted. Although I insisted on being heard out, he said, "This will suffice."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statements that you made to the Bosnia-Herzegovina authorities, the investigators -- were the investigators asking you questions and then did you answer, or did you give a spontaneous statement that the investigators noted down, or did things occur in a different way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: All of this happened spontaneously. I must tell you, though, that had I given a statement before I was taken to Batkovic, as soon as I was released from Luka, it would have been more precise and detailed. However, we were taken to the camp in order to be brainwashed. We ate food without any salt over there, very small quantities at that, and that, in addition to time, has affected our memory. So I could not remember everything when I was exchanged from the Batkovic camp. As a person thinks about what had happened, he remembers these details as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Witness I. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have only one question to ask. After all of these ordeals that you went through at the Luka camp, in the end what is your definitive impression that the accused played? Did he give you the impression of directing the operations or of simply being someone who carried things out? Could you give us some specifics about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: I could say that he was both. He carried out orders but he also selected his victims through his own free will. He could have not shot dead someone even if he were told to do so, but he did quite a few things on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS I
utterances.text: For example -- for example, he didn't have to beat people so badly with such big batons. If he was supposed to kill a man, he could have killed him immediately, but he would kill him with an object, a baton or a stick or something, and then finally he would cut his suffering short; he would shoot him finally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have finished. You have shown a great deal of patience and the Tribunal expresses all its gratitude to you. We will take some precautions before the next witness is brought in. The blinds have to be drawn and the Victims and Witnesses Section will take care of you. We wish you a calm return. You have done your duty. You've shown a great deal of courage in doing so, and you did, and we are grateful to you for that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, that's enough. I don't think there's anybody there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put on the microphones, please. Do you hear me? Mr. Usher, he can't answer. You've got to turn the microphone on. How do you expect me to speak to him? How do you expect him to answer me? Do you hear me? You should have let him remain seated. All right. You have to read your solemn declaration now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. We're going to call you Witness J because you are a witness who is covered by protective measures which the Tribunal has ordered. Thank you for having come. First you're going to be asked questions by the Prosecutor. I'm sure he will explain how this is going to take place. Most likely tomorrow you will be asked questions by Defence counsel for the accused. This is the trial initiated by the Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic, who is present, to your left, in this courtroom. I see Mr. Nice is going to conduct the examination-in-chief. Please proceed, Mr. Nice. The identity of the witness. Please show him the piece of paper to show that he can recognise his name. But don't state your name. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness J, have you considered a summary of your potential evidence now before you, and is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the conflict, did you work as an economist for a company?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 30th of April of 1992, were you with your family in Klanac, a predominantly Muslim area, but did you move on the 3rd of May to Kolobara, where you were for a time in the basement of another house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, were you arrested by Serb soldiers, some in JNA uniforms and some in the blue uniforms of the Civilian Protection Forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you separated, men from women, and the men taken to the mosque, your estimate of the number of men in the mosque being that there were how many there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Up to 200 at the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the mosque, were you guarded by uniformed men, some of whom you thought you could identify as to their organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that organisation you thought was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which groups did you think they were a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: There were several groups. One belonged to Arkan's soldiers, the others were the so-called White Eagles, and other different soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. When you give your answer, please try to face the Judges, Witness J. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay at the mosque, were some people interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, what type of people or what -- yes. What people were interrogated while at the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I mostly remember Papa having been interrogated, that is actually Ahmet Hodzic, and a few other younger men whom I knew but not by their names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Papa having, before the conflict, been associated with the local SDA as its chairman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He was the president of the local community of Kolobara and a member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a young man there who tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes. That was Zikret Suljic, nicknamed Kike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him when he tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: In that general commotion, a soldier, who I think belonged to Arkan's soldiers, judging by his uniform, he ordered us to lie on the ground, and he shot a round at him. He shot him in the back when he had already reached the window of the mosque, using one single round only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you moved from the mosque to another location? If so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, I was moved, together with about 15 other citizens, to the military barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't actually asked this witness to look at this map beforehand, but if he can help us with it, then the Court will be able to have a map which will throw some further light on the case you're dealing with. Can the witness have this one for the ELMO? There are larger, rather more convenient-sized maps for the Court and for my learned friends opposite. If this witness cannot deal with the map, then I will get another witness who can.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 33.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to read maps, Witness J?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's only one copy. I wonder whether it would be possible to have a second copy between the two of us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm most grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness J, can you read maps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you would put the river at the top, that's the way around. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness J, can you be given, please, the pointer? When you're pointing things out to us, will you stay in your seat so that your identity is not revealed. Use the pointer. If you point something out on the map, not on the screen, if you point it out on the device to your right-hand side where the usher is indicating, we'll see it on the screen. Very quickly, because the Judges have yet to see, I think, a map, unless I'm mistaken in my memory, does this show the river running from northwest to the east with what was the main bridge across it? Just point to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you're able here to show us where the mosque was. If yes, point to it; if not, I'll get that dealt with in another way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He indicates an area towards the top left of the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The barracks to which you had moved, where are they to be found? It may be that we will need to have the bottom part of the map in view. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're indicating an area in the middle of the town. There is, we see, on the map, right at the bottom right-hand corner, another area that's marked as army barracks, but those weren't the barracks to which you were taken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We will leave the map on the ELMO because I will refer to it again in a minute. You were taken to the barracks, and were other men from areas of Brcko and elsewhere also brought there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In particular, from what other area did men arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Most were from Brcko Novo, Mujkici, Meraje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are those areas? Are they areas of particular ethnic composition or, to be precise, were they areas of particular ethnic composition at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Brcko Novo is a mixed neighbourhood, and Meraje and Mujkici were predominantly Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mujkici in Brcko or is it in an area outside Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, it's approximately about 1.000 metres away from the mosque where we were. It's by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The stadium, I think we can see on this map. At least I can see one stadium on it. Can you see the stadium on this map, which is near to Mujkici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It's in the top left-hand corner. Thank you. Following your move to the barracks and, indeed, on the following day, did you volunteer to do something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: To clean up glass around the SUP building from the effects of the detonation after the bridge had exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can just move the plan down a bit so that we can see the bridge. It may not be possible with a plan of this scale to identify precisely where the centre of town was, but we can see where the bridge that was blown up was. Can you point out roughly where it was that you went in order to clear up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this aerial view show that part of the town to which you went when you went as a volunteer to clear up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you volunteer to go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Until then, I wasn't aware that a war had started and what I'd got into, and I thought I might thus reach the Sava and cross it and get away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at this photograph, can you point out the police station there, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes, I do. [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That building we see, and this is for purposes of orientating ourselves for the next photograph, has in the front of it three trees. Do you see those three trees, the one on the left and then two trees to the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look, please, at the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this photograph show on the right-hand side the police station and then, substantially in the middle of the photograph, those same two trees that we were looking at from the aerial view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning mentally to the aerial view, this is looking from the top of the photograph down towards the police station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the town to clear up, did you go into that police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Not immediately, not my group. A group did go in, about 10 of them, and about 17 of us stayed outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subsequently, did you go into that police station and, indeed, were you interrogated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went in or while you were inside, did you hear something and did things happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: When I entered the last room on the first floor, escorted by two men in camouflage uniforms, I heard gunfire outside, so that those two soldiers left that office where I was. They ran out and I also tried to run out after them; that is, I left that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see on your way out or on leaving?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Midway down the passage, Senad Muranjkovic called. Petar was lying there and he was holding his leg, and I could see that he was wounded. In the adjacent room, to the left-hand side as you enter, there was Sead Karagic also lying down. Half of his body was in the room and his legs were outside, and he had a mason's hatchet in his back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those two of the men with whom you'd been associated in coming to town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a third man, Hasan Jasarevic, who had been in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He must have entered and got scared and tried to escape from the building, and they fired because he was trying to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything of his attempt to escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was in that room; that is, in that last room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you just answer this "Yes" or "No": Were you told what happened to him; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Guys who were clearing up outside, who were not inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they tell you had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: They said that he'd been caught in front of Oslobodenje kiosk and that Goran Jelisic had taken him down to Agro Banka, between SUP and Agro Banka, and that there he shot him dead, with one bullet fired at the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at the photograph still on the ELMO screen, does that show the kiosk and/or does that show the bank? If so, please point them out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The kiosk is here [Indicating], and you can't see the bank for these, but that is where it should be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can see the word "Banka" just on top of it. Thank you. After that incident at the police station, what did you do? Did you go back to complete the interrogation, did you go to carry on clearing up, or what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I went on clearing up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the area were you clearing and how were you doing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I was clearing up here [Indicating], this street here, from the SUP entrance to the kiosk and to the Oslobodenje cinema; that is, the former cinema.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness please have the previous photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, by use of the pointer, show us what area of the street you were clearing of whatever you were clearing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. While you were doing that, did you see something of a man from Sinteraj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he? What was he doing? What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: He was here [indicating] at the moment when I saw him. I was clearing up here, and he was moving down the street, escorted by two policemen walking on his sides and Goran following.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you know who either of these policemen were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, indeed, at that time, although you've used the name Goran, did you know who Goran was, or did you get to know him at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I met him later or, rather, he introduced himself to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Later, later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the next photograph? But leave that photograph on the ELMO for the time being, if you would be so good.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 36.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we put this photograph on the ELMO, can you just stay with the existing aerial view, and can you follow the road you were sweeping towards the left? And then can you trace a lane that runs down on the aerial view with your pointer and tell us what that lane contains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: SUP, Oslobodenje cinema, the Posavina Hotel, the crafts centre, the barbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's on the lane going down from that junction that you've just crossed? What's on that little lane there, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This one here [indicating], you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, the other one. I'm going down on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This here [indicating]?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Down.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: This one goes towards the Sava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Perhaps you can have a look at the next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just lay that one on top of it, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that street or lane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the buildings on the right-hand side of it, which are comparatively modern than the buildings on the left, can you now, please, go back to the previous photograph, if the usher would be good enough to take the top one off, and tell us where you think that lane is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: [Indicating]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we now have a photograph of that lane. When you saw the man with the two police officers and the man who was subsequently to introduce himself as Goran, where were they going, and then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: They were moving towards this small street, towards this lane next to the craft centre, and a shot could be heard, and then Goran came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the young man come back or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later see a vehicle driving to the area where you'd seen the young man go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: It was a refrigerator truck of the Bimeks company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it go into that lane or just to the mouth of the lane or somewhere else? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I'm not really quite certain whether it was he entered, but I know he went down there. I could not really look how the vehicle moved, but I know he went in the direction of that street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you'd seen following the two policemen and the young man, how was it that he introduced himself to you? Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, as I worked, he often -- as a matter of fact, I didn't know it was Goran, but we come and go. At some moment he lined us up here in front of the SUP entrance, in three lines, and ordered us to look at this flag and sing Serb songs, I think, march songs or national songs. Then he was sitting on a wooden chair, and told us that he was Goran Jelisic, called "Serb Adolf," and that we should remember that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you was it that he had singing to the Serb flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Fifteen, sixteen, or thereabouts. It depended. Some people remained longer in the upper part of the building, that is, cleaning the windows of the showers and things like that, but we were some 15 or 16 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first interrogation that you had had been interrupted by what had happened outside or both inside and outside the police station. Were you interrogated again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: I said I was not interrogated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: If I may say, at the beginning I was interrogated by Goran but I did not know his name at the time. It was in the beginning, and it was by Goran and a policeman in a blue uniform. As we carried the splinters, the glass, they intercepted us and told us to put the glass down and said, "Let's talk about SDA, young Muslims, ZNGs and the like." After that they took us into the SUP building, but that was right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Well, then I must ask you a little bit more about that. When you were interrogated or questioned by Goran, what did he say? What, if anything, did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: During the interrogation, as I did not tell them anything, he beat me with his baton on my shoulders and on the head, and after a stronger blow I put my hand up to shield myself, and he hit me here on the knuckles and injured me. As the baton fell down -- flew down, of course he cursed my balija mother, how dare I raise my hand against him, and I believe four bullets fell out of his reserve magazine, I think, which he had on his belt. He ordered the soldiers to remove me away, and promised me that I'd be the last one to be killed in that group because I could carry that glass [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you carry -- what was it you were able to carry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: The dead ones. The dead ones which I guess he planned killing that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to be quite sure about, insofar as you can help us, the location of things in order, this questioning by Goran and his saying you were going to be the last one to be killed occurred right at the beginning, before there had been the commotion at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was after that that you went and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Before. It was before the commotion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So after that you went and swept the streets, and after that you saw the young man from Sinteraj go down the lane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also see something that day of a man known as Papa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before or after your interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: After the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing at the time and what did you see, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS J
utterances.text: Well, I was sweeping the street right there in front of the building, and I saw him come out from the SUP building with a hand bandaged and visibly limping on one foot. So he was moving slowly. Goran followed after him, and there were two soldiers, one on each side, escorting him. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was simply looking at what time it is. I think the interpreters are tired and, in any case, since you won't be able to finish this afternoon, I think, Mr. Nice, that it might be a point to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have to deal with the list, which always takes some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we resume tomorrow at 2.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The hearing will resume tomorrow. Witness J, we wish you a good evening, and you will be properly taken care of. We will resume tomorrow again, at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 5.37 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of September, 1999 at 2.00 p.m. 22 23 24 25
